rationale: Both address the son by commanding attention to the speaker's words and an inclined ear.
Guarding good understanding corresponds to good counsel and holy thought guarding the learner.
Honey dripping from lips describes seductive danger here but the bride's welcome sweetness in the Song.
The seduction that ends in bitterness corresponds to the entrapping woman found more bitter than death.
Folly's course leads her companions down with death into Hades in the source; the target depicts personified evil counsel with a house beside death and courses beside Hades.
Folly's slippery tracks exclude life's ways in the source; the target says that those traveling in personified evil counsel fail to regain straight paths or years of life.
Both appeal to a child to listen and refuse to reject the teacher's counsel.
Joseph refuses repeated sexual invitations and flees the woman's grasp, illustrating deliberate distance from seduction.
Surrendering one's life to the merciless corresponds to the married woman's hunt for men's precious lives.
The loss of one's labor and strength to outsiders corresponds to wealth destroyed through association with prostitutes.
The body's eventual wasting belongs to the same warning as adultery bringing destruction on one's own life.
The confession of hating discipline and rebukes exemplifies the foolish hatred of rebukes condemned in the target.
The refusal to listen to teachers repeats the refusal to heed Wisdom's calls, counsel and reproofs.
Both place sexual wrongdoing before an assembly; Sirach describes the adulterous woman brought before it and visitation upon her children.
The chapter's marriage instruction uses one's own spring and well, while the Song describes the bride as a sealed fountain and living-water well.
The restriction of spring water to one's own sphere corresponds to the warning against drinking from a foreign spring.
The exclusion of an outsider from the marriage-water image corresponds to the lovers' declaration of mutual belonging.
Sharing joy with the wife of one's youth corresponds to enjoying life with the woman one has loved throughout one's days.
Continuing in one's own woman's affection corresponds to enjoying life with the beloved woman throughout one's days.
The prohibition of embracing another woman corresponds to honoring marriage and keeping its bed undefiled.
God's observation of every human track directly answers the adulterer's claim that darkness and walls conceal his sin.
Being bound by one's own sins corresponds to lawless people caught in their own destruction.
Death through lack of discipline corresponds to the shameful death of those who hate rebukes.
Both warn that giving oneself as a pledge endangers one's security and possessions.
Both describe one's own lips or mouth as a trap for one's life.
Urgently seeking release from a guarantee answers the danger that an unpaid pledge can cost even one's bedding.
Escaping like hunted animals corresponds to the righteous escaping from the hunt.
Both present the small ant as an example of wisdom because it prepares food in summer.
The ant acts without a master, while the locust marches in order without a king; both use creatures lacking these forms of authority as examples of resourcefulness.
Both explicitly describe ants preparing their food in summer.
Both commend the bee through the value of what she produces, with Proverbs emphasizing her industrious labor.
The bee's widely valued produce corresponds to her product being foremost among sweet things; Sirach does not make the health claim.
The weak bee's advancement through wisdom parallels Sirach's movement from wisdom exalting the humble to the small bee's excellent product.
The summons to a sleeping sluggard accords with the warning that an idle person's life will hunger.
Both repeat the sluggard's little sleep, little dozing and clasped hands.
Both describe poverty arriving and want coming like a good runner after habitual idleness.
Diligence bringing harvest and dismissing want corresponds to abundance coming through taking care rather than pleasure-loving neglect.
The lawless man's bad ways correspond to a lawless companion who leads friends into ways that are not good.
Deceptive eye signals recur in the target, where they gather grief for others.
A twisted heart continually devising evils corresponds to deceit in the heart of one devising evil things.
Both threaten sudden destruction with no healing, here for the deviser of evil and there for the stiff-necked person.
Rejoicing in what the Lord hates corresponds to people delighting in evils and rejoicing in distortion.
The condemnation of hands shedding righteous blood corresponds to the gang's plan to kill a righteous man and its haste to shed blood.
The evil-designing heart corresponds to the heart as the source of evil reasonings, murder and other sins.
Both identify the unjust witness as one who kindles lies or falsehoods.
Both command the son to heed his father and not reject his mother's ordinances.
Fastening instruction to the soul and neck corresponds to keeping commanded words in heart and soul and binding them on the hand.
Both place instruction alongside walking, lying down and rising, making it a continual companion.
The commandment as lamp and light corresponds to God's word lighting the feet and paths.
Both describe instruction or wisdom as protection against a dangerous woman, while depicting the threat of her speech differently.
The warning against desire through one's eyes corresponds to Jesus' warning about lustful looking and the eye that causes stumbling.
The woman hunting precious lives corresponds to the woman whose heart is nets and whose hands are bonds.
Fire held close to the body illustrates sexual danger here; Sirach likewise portrays uncontrolled sexual desire as consuming fire.
The unavoidable burns from coals reinforce the image of sexual desire as a fire that continues until consumption.
The warning that one who touches a married woman will not be acquitted corresponds to God's judgment of adulterers.
Proverbs explains a hungry thief's motive without canceling restitution, while Ephesians directs the thief to cease stealing and work for others' needs.
The thief gives possessions to rescue himself, illustrating the target's observation that one's wealth can ransom one's life.
Adultery destroying one's own life corresponds to sexual immorality being a sin against one's own body.
Both describe sexual wrongdoing leaving a reproach that will not be erased.
The husband's fierce jealousy corresponds to the Song's description of jealousy as harsh as Hades; the Song is not itself an adultery judgment.
The husband's refusal of ransom qualifies the observation that wealth can ransom a life: money cannot resolve this adulterous injury.
Hiding commandments within oneself corresponds to hiding God's sayings in the heart to avoid sin.
Honoring the Lord as the source of strength corresponds to hope of strength in the fear of the Lord.
Guarding commandments in order to live corresponds to holding discipline fast for one's life.
Commandments placed around fingers and inscribed on the heart correspond to words kept in heart and soul and bound on the hand.
Wisdom is welcomed as a sister and intimate companion here, and sought as a beloved bride in the target.
Both explain instruction's protective role against a dangerous woman and her speech.
The youth lacking sense exemplifies the innocent person who believes every word instead of reconsidering.
The youth passing by her house does the opposite of the instruction to keep far from her doors.
Night supplies the setting for the encounter, while Sirach exposes the adulterer's belief that darkness will hide him.
Both women physically seize the man while pressing a sexual invitation; Joseph's flight contrasts with the youth's later submission.
The seductress's claim to have a peace sacrifice and be paying vows is exposed by the principle that impious people's sacrifices are detestable.
Saffron and cinnamon furnish erotic fragrance in both passages, here as part of an adulterous invitation and there in the lover's garden imagery.
The invitation to adulterous affection contrasts with the command to rejoice with one's own wife and avoid another woman's arms.
An absent husband is offered as an opportunity for adultery here, while an empty household supplies the opportunity for the attempted seduction of Joseph.
The woman's persuasive conversation realizes the danger described as sweetness dripping from a prostitute's lips.
Following her like an animal to slaughter illustrates lawless conduct taking away the participant's own life.
The bird rushing into a trap corresponds to the entrapping woman's nets and bonds that catch the sinner.
Both command the son to listen and attend to the speaker's utterances.
The warning against turning the heart toward her ways corresponds to identifying adultery already in the lustful heart.
The woman's many slain victims exemplify the earlier warning that folly leads her companions down with death into Hades.
The woman's house leads to Hades and death in the source; the target gives personified evil counsel a house beside death and courses beside Hades.
The call to proclaim wisdom corresponds to Wisdom being publicly celebrated and speaking in the squares.
Wisdom's elevated position on summits corresponds to her proclamation from the tops of walls.
Both explicitly place Wisdom beside rulers' gates and city entrances.
Wisdom's public address to humankind corresponds to her opening her mouth before her people and the assembly.
Wisdom's summons for innocent people to learn resourcefulness matches the stated purpose of giving shrewdness to the innocent.
Wisdom's noble and upright sayings correspond to the noble sayings of pure people.
Both reject lying lips as detestable, here before Wisdom and there before the Lord.
Both describe righteousness proceeding from Wisdom's mouth.
Wisdom's words being plain to the understanding corresponds to discernment being readily found among intelligent people.
Both prefer wisdom or understanding to gold and silver.
Both rank wisdom above a costly stone and precious metals.
Wisdom's dwelling with counsel, knowledge and reflection corresponds to wisdom and perception bringing protective counsel and thought into the learner.
The fear of the Lord expressed as hatred of evil corresponds to fearing God and turning from every evil.
Wisdom's possession of counsel, understanding and strength corresponds to her mighty and competent government of all things.
Kings' dependence on wisdom corresponds to the chosen king's request for wisdom, without which even an otherwise perfect ruler counts as nothing.
Ruling through wisdom corresponds to humanity being fashioned through God's wisdom to rule and render righteous judgment.
Wisdom's promise to be found by seekers corresponds to tracing her out until she becomes known and holding her fast.
Both explicitly place wealth and glory with Wisdom.
Wisdom's produce outranking gold and silver corresponds to counting wealth as nothing and metals as sand or clay beside her.
Wisdom's righteous and just paths correspond to her teaching righteousness, understanding and self-control.
Wisdom filling her lovers' storehouses corresponds to good things and immeasurable wealth coming with her.
Wisdom's account of daily happenings and eternity corresponds to her knowledge of ancient things and the outcomes of times.
Both personified Wisdom passages explicitly speak of her being created from the beginning; this comparison preserves their wording without settling later doctrinal interpretation.
Both locate Wisdom before the age and from the beginning.
Wisdom speaks of preceding earth and deeps, while Genesis presents earth, deep and waters at the beginning of creation.
Wisdom precedes the mountains and hills here, while the psalm depicts mountains rising to the place God founded for them.
The Lord's making lands and inhabited extremities corresponds to the appearance and naming of the dry land as earth.
Preparing heaven and marking a throne upon winds corresponds to stretching out heaven and walking on the wings of winds.
The ordering of clouds and water springs corresponds to God's understanding splitting deeps and causing clouds to flow with dew.
Both describe God making or laying the earth's foundations.
Wisdom beside God during His works corresponds to Wisdom present with Him when He made the world.
God's delight in the completed inhabited world and humankind corresponds to the creation of humans and His judgment that all He made was very good.
Both directly summon a child to listen to instruction.
Daily attendance at Wisdom's doors corresponds to rising early to visit an understanding teacher and wearing down his doorstep.
Wisdom's ways leading out to life correspond to her being a tree of life for those holding her fast.
Rejecting Wisdom harms one's own life, just as thrusting discipline away is described as hating oneself.
Wisdom building her house corresponds to wise women building houses, in contrast to foolish destruction.
Wisdom's prepared table corresponds to the host's great supper, whose readiness is announced to invited guests.
Wisdom sends servants to summon guests to her prepared meal, as the host sends a servant to announce that the banquet is ready.
Wisdom invites the foolish and those lacking understanding, matching her summons to innocent and uneducated hearers.
The invitation to consume Wisdom's bread and wine corresponds to God's invitation to receive food and wine and listen so that life may follow.
Abandoning folly and seeking understanding in order to live corresponds to understanding's ways of life that turn aside from Hades.
Reproof brings dishonor from evil recipients, just as the uneducated person refuses to love reprovers or associate with the wise.
The wise person's love for a reprover corresponds to love of discipline, whereas the evil person's hatred corresponds to foolish hatred of rebukes.
Both say that a wise listener becomes still wiser through further instruction.
Both explicitly identify fear of God or the Lord as the beginning of wisdom.
Both state that knowing the law belongs to a good mind.
Both promise added length of life and years through receiving instruction.
The learner bears the effects of wisdom or evil, as the merciful person benefits his own life and the merciless person destroys his body.
Leaning on lies and chasing winds or birds corresponds to wealth won by false speech pursuing empty things toward death's traps.
Abandoning one's vineyard and field contrasts with working one's own land for food rather than pursuing empty things.
The wanderer's fruitless wilderness corresponds to the neglected field or vineyard becoming wasteland; both portray unproductive consequences of folly.
Folly takes a conspicuous seat at her doorway, imitating Wisdom's public seat at rulers' gates.
Folly calls to people passing on straight ways, countering Wisdom's public summons to humankind.
Folly repeats Wisdom's invitation for the foolish to turn aside, making the rival offers deliberately alike while their outcomes differ.
Pleasure in hidden bread and stolen water corresponds to the sexually immoral man's sweet loaves and imagined security in concealment.
Folly's visitor comes upon Hades where earth-born ones perish; the target likewise places personified evil counsel's courses beside Hades with the earthborn.
The command to leap away and not linger is illustrated by Joseph leaving his garment and fleeing the attempted seduction.
Avoiding a foreign spring directly contrasts with drinking from one's own vessels and spring wells.
Both promise that heeding instruction will add length of life and years.
Both say a wise son gladdens his father and contrast the foolish son's injury to his mother.
Righteousness rescuing from death corresponds to righteousness rescuing the upright while lawless people are caught in destruction.
The Lord sustaining a righteous life contrasts with impious deprivation, as the righteous eat to fullness while the impious remain in want.
Both associate courageous people with wealth: their hands make rich in the source, while they lean upon wealth in the target, which contrasts them with the lazy lacking wealth.
The disciplined wise son having the fool as a servant corresponds to the fool serving an intelligent person.
Both explicitly place the Lord's blessing upon the righteous person's head, with the target expanding its freedom from sorrow.
The righteous person's praised memory corresponds to regret at his death, while the impious person's disappearance corresponds to welcomed destruction.
Unrestrained lips bringing a fall correspond to rash lips imperiling their owner while guarded speech preserves life.
Sincere conduct bringing confidence corresponds to the righteous person's lion-like confidence, contrasted with the impious person's fear.
The deceitful eye signal that brings grief corresponds to gestures used by the twisted-hearted person who devises evil and stirs civic disturbances.
A fountain of life associated with the righteous corresponds to the wise person's life-giving law, opposed to death's traps.
Friendship covering people opposed to strife corresponds to seeking friendship by hiding wrongdoings instead of separating friends.
Both join speech with a rod or staff: the source's wise speaker strikes the man lacking heart with a rod, while the target pictures a staff of insolence issuing from fools' mouths.
The rash mouth approaching ruin corresponds to rash lips endangering their owner, opposed to guarding one's mouth.
Both call the rich person's property a fortified city.
Righteous work producing life corresponds to a tree of life growing from righteousness's fruit.
Discipline guarding paths of life corresponds to holding discipline fast for one's own life.
The condemnation of abusive speech corresponds to removing slander and malice and practicing kind forgiveness; it does not require treating concealed enmity as endorsed by Ephesians.
Sparing one's lips to avoid sin corresponds to guarding one's mouth to keep one's life.
The righteous tongue is compared to fire-tested silver, the same image used for the purity of the Lord's sayings in the psalm.
Righteous lips knowing lofty things correspond to wise lips bound to discernment, while foolish hearts lack security.
The Lord's blessing on the righteous corresponds to God's blessing of righteous dwellings rather than His curse on the impious household.
The fool laughing while doing evil corresponds to people who delight in evils and rejoice in distortion.
The acceptable desire of the righteous corresponds to every righteous desire being good, contrasted with the impious person's failed hope.
The impious disappearing while the righteous survives corresponds to the impious disappearing wherever he turns while righteous houses remain.
Lawlessness harming its practitioners corresponds to lawless deeds taking away the doer's own life.
Fear of the Lord adding days corresponds to the added years promised in Wisdom's instruction following the fear-of-the-Lord saying.
The source's perishing impious hope corresponds to the target's perishing impious boast, contrasted with continuing gladness or hope for the righteous.
Fear of the Lord as a stronghold for the devout corresponds to hope of strength and support in that fear.
Both contrast the righteous remaining in the land with the impious or lawless being removed from it.
Righteous speech producing wisdom corresponds to the wise tongue knowing good things, contrasted with the impious or foolish mouth.
Righteous lips producing gracious things correspond to speaking what builds others up and gives grace to hearers.
